summary.text: For each prime, positive-semidefinite congruence-versus-opposite-congruence kernels are signed by residue classes to convert valuation inequalities into an energy bound \(\sum_{a,b}(\log a+\log b-2\log\gcd(a,b))\le 4r^2|A|\log(2H)\), where \(r\) counts the pair-sum primes and \(H=\max A\). Choosing \(r+2\) low-distance anchors, normalizing by their gcd, and applying an excess-prime pigeonhole argument bounds the height of the entire primitive set in terms of the anchors; eliminating the height gives \(|A|\le 65(r+1)^5\), from which the superlogarithmic growth follows.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 P(A):=\prod_{(a,b)\in A^2,\ a\ne b}(a+b)
\]
(the product is over ordered off-diagonal pairs), and let
\[
 r(A):=\omega(P(A))
\]
be the number of distinct prime divisors of this product. We will prove the following stronger uniform estimate:
\[
 |A|\le 65\bigl(r(A)+1\bigr)^5                                      \tag{1}
\]
for every finite set \(A\subseteq\mathbb N\). Once (1) is known, the desired limit follows readily.

Throughout, \(v_p(n)\) denotes the exponent of the prime \(p\) in a positive integer \(n\), and \(|a-b|\) denotes the ordinary nonnegative distance between natural numbers.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
1. A quadratic sign-unwinding principle
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

For a finite index set \(I\), a real matrix \(M=(M_{ij})_{i,j\in I}\), and a vector \(c=(c_i)\), write
\[
 Q_M(c)=\sum_{i,j\in I}c_i c_jM_{ij}.
\]
Call \(M\) positive semidefinite if \(Q_M(c)\ge0\) for every real vector \(c\).

We need the following elementary fact. Suppose \(M\) is positive semidefinite, its off-diagonal entries are nonpositive, and \(M_{ii}\le D\) for every \(i\). Then
\[
 Q_M(c)\le 2D\sum_i c_i^2.                                           \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, compare \(Q_M(c)\) with \(Q_M(|c|)\). If \(i\ne j\), then
\[
 c_ic_j+|c_i||c_j|\ge0,
\]
so multiplication by \(M_{ij}\le0\) gives a nonpositive contribution. On the diagonal, the combined contribution is
\(2c_i^2M_{ii}\le2Dc_i^2\). Thus
\[
 Q_M(c)+Q_M(|c|)\le2D\sum_i c_i^2.
\]
Since \(Q_M(|c|)\ge0\), (2) follows.

A consequence that will be used below is the following. Let \(M_p\), indexed by a finite set \(S\), be positive semidefinite matrices on the same finite set \(I\). Assume that
\[
 \sum_{p\in S}(M_p)_{ij}\le0\quad(i\ne j),
 \qquad
 \sum_{p\in S}(M_p)_{ii}\le D.
\]
For every \(p\), let \(\sigma_p(i)\in\{1,-1\}\). Then
\[
 \sum_{p\in S}\sum_{i,j\in I}
 \sigma_p(i)\sigma_p(j)(M_p)_{ij}
 \le 2|S|D|I|.                                                       \tag{3}
\]
To see this, fix \(p\). Since all the other \(M_q\) are positive semidefinite,
\[
 Q_{M_p}(\sigma_p)\le Q_{\sum_qM_q}(\sigma_p).
\]
Apply (2) to \(\sum_qM_q\), noting that \(\sum_i\sigma_p(i)^2=|I|\), and then sum over \(p\).

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Prime-adic congruence kernels
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

For a modulus \(q>0\), consider the matrix
\[
 K_q(a,b)=\mathbf 1_{q\mid |a-b|}-\mathbf 1_{q\mid a+b}.
\]
This matrix is positive semidefinite on any finite family of natural numbers. Here is a direct proof. Group coefficients \(c_a\) according to their residue classes modulo \(q\), and put
\[
 C_x=\sum_{a\equiv x\pmod q}c_a.
\]
Then
\[
 \sum_{a,b}c_ac_b\mathbf1_{a\equiv b\pmod q}=\sum_xC_x^2,

a\qquad
 \sum_{a,b}c_ac_b\mathbf1_{a\equiv-b\pmod q}=\sum_xC_xC_{-x}.
\]
Consequently the quadratic form of \(K_q\) is
\[
 \sum_x C_x^2-\sum_xC_xC_{-x}\ge0,
\]
because \(2C_xC_{-x}\le C_x^2+C_{-x}^2\), and \(x\mapsto-x\) permutes the residue classes.

For a prime \(p\) and an integer \(K\ge0\), define the truncated valuation kernel
\[
 T_{p,K}(a,b)
 =\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}
 \left(\mathbf1_{p^{k+1}\mid |a-b|}-
       \mathbf1_{p^{k+1}\mid a+b}\right).                           \tag{4}
\]
It is a sum of the preceding positive semidefinite kernels, hence is positive semidefinite. If \(a\ne b\), \(a+b>0\), and both relevant valuations are at most \(K\), then
\[
 T_{p,K}(a,b)=v_p(|a-b|)-v_p(a+b).                                   \tag{5}
\]
This follows because the number of integers \(k\in\{0,\dots,K-1\}\) for which \(p^{k+1}\mid n\) is \(\min(K,v_p(n))\). On the diagonal, since every power of \(p\) divides \(0=|a-a|\), each summand in (4) is either \(0\) or \(1\), and therefore
\[
 0\le T_{p,K}(a,a)\le K.                                            \tag{6}
\]

We next choose signs which turn the valuation difference in (5) into useful information about \(v_p(a+b)\). For odd \(p\), divide the nonzero residue classes modulo \(p\) into the lower and upper halves; for \(p=2\), use the two halves modulo \(4\). Let \(\varepsilon_p(u)\in\{1,-1\}\) record in which half the residue of \(u\) lies. If \(p\nmid u,v\), then the following inequality holds:
\[
 v_p(u+v)-v_p(2)
 \le \varepsilon_p(u)\varepsilon_p(v)
       \bigl(v_p(|u-v|)-v_p(u+v)\bigr).                              \tag{7}
\]
There are two cases. If \(u,v\) have the same color, then \(v_p(u+v)\le v_p(2)\): for odd \(p\), two residues in the same half cannot be nonzero opposites modulo \(p\); for \(p=2\), two odd residues in the same half modulo \(4\) cannot have sum divisible by \(4\). The left side of (7) is therefore nonpositive, while the sign product is \(+1\); also \(v_p(|u-v|)\ge v_p(2)\) (the only nontrivial assertion is that the difference of two odd numbers is even). This proves (7) in this case. If the colors differ, then the sign product is \(-1\), and the color definition implies \(v_p(|u-v|)\le v_p(2)\); rearranging gives (7).

For a general positive integer \(a\), remove its \(p\)-power part and set
\[
 a_p^*=a/p^{v_p(a)},\qquad \sigma_p(a)=\varepsilon_p(a_p^*).
\]
Then \(\sigma_p(a)^2=1\). We claim that, for distinct positive \(a,b\),
\[
 v_p(a+b)-v_p(\gcd(a,b))-v_p(2)
 \le \sigma_p(a)\sigma_p(b)
       \bigl(v_p(|a-b|)-v_p(a+b)\bigr).                              \tag{8}
\]
If \(v_p(a)\ne v_p(b)\), the standard unequal-valuation rule gives
\[
 v_p(a+b)=v_p(|a-b|)=\min(v_p(a),v_p(b))=v_p(\gcd(a,b)).
\]
Thus the right side of (8) is zero and the left side is \(-v_p(2)\le0\). If \(v_p(a)=v_p(b)=e\), write \(a=p^eu\), \(b=p^ev\), where \(p\nmid u,v\). Then both \(v_p(a+b)\) and \(v_p(|a-b|)\) acquire the same additive term \(e\), while \(v_p(\gcd(a,b))=e\). Inequality (8) is exactly (7) for \(u,v\).

Combining (5) and (8), whenever the truncation level is at least both valuations, gives
\[
 v_p(a+b)-v_p(\gcd(a,b))-v_p(2)
 \le \sigma_p(a)\sigma_p(b)T_{p,K}(a,b).                            \tag{9}
\]

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
3. The logarithmic gcd-distance energy bound
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

For positive integers define
\[
 d(a,b)=\log a+\log b-2\log\gcd(a,b).
\]
This is nonnegative, because \(\gcd(a,b)\le a,b\), and \(d(a,a)=0\). The arithmetic-geometric mean inequality \(4ab\le(a+b)^2\) gives
\[
 \log a+\log b\le2(\log(a+b)-\log2),
\]
and therefore
\[
 d(a,b)\le2\bigl(\log(a+b)-\log\gcd(a,b)-\log2\bigr).             \tag{10}
\]

Let \(A\) be a finite set of positive integers, all at most \(H\), where \(H>0\). Let \(S\) be a finite set of primes such that every prime divisor of every off-diagonal sum \(a+b\) belongs to \(S\). Put \(s=|S|\). We prove
\[
 \sum_{a,b\in A}d(a,b)
 \le4s^2|A|\log(2H).                                                 \tag{11}
\]

For each \(p\in S\), choose
\[
 K_p=\lfloor\log_p(2H)\rfloor

a\]
in the integer sense, so that \(p^{K_p}\le2H<p^{K_p+1}\), and define
\[
 M_p(a,b)=(\log p)T_{p,K_p}(a,b).
\]
Since \(|a-b|\le2H\) and \(a+b\le2H\), their \(p\)-adic valuations are at most \(K_p\). Thus (5) applies off the diagonal.

Each \(M_p\) is positive semidefinite. For \(a\ne b\),
\[
 \sum_{p\in S}M_p(a,b)
 =\sum_{p\in S}v_p(|a-b|)\log p-\log(a+b)\le0.                      \tag{12}
\]
Here the second sum is exactly \(\log(a+b)\), because all prime factors of \(a+b\) lie in \(S\), while the first is at most the full prime-factorization sum \(\log|a-b|\le\log(a+b)\).

By (6),
\[
 M_p(a,a)\le K_p\log p\le\log(2H),
\]
so
\[
 \sum_{p\in S}M_p(a,a)\le s\log(2H).                               \tag{13}
\]
Applying (3), with \(D=s\log(2H)\), gives
\[
 \sum_{p\in S}\sum_{a,b\in A}
 \sigma_p(a)\sigma_p(b)M_p(a,b)
 \le2s^2|A|\log(2H).                                                \tag{14}
\]

For distinct \(a,b\), sum (9), after multiplication by \(\log p\), over \(p\in S\). The contribution from \(a+b\) is exactly \(\log(a+b)\). The partial sums for \(\gcd(a,b)\) and for \(2\) are at most \(\log\gcd(a,b)\) and \(\log2\), respectively. Hence the signed sum on the right is at least
\[
 \log(a+b)-\log\gcd(a,b)-\log2,
\]
which by (10) is at least \(d(a,b)/2\). The same inequality is harmless on the diagonal because \(d(a,a)=0\) and the signed diagonal contribution is nonnegative. Summing and using (14) proves (11).

We record an immediate row-average consequence. Taking
\(S\) to be the full prime support of \(P(A)\), so \(s=r(A)\), there is some \(a\in A\) such that
\[
 \sum_{b\in A}d(a,b)\le4r(A)^2\log(2H).                             \tag{15}
\]
Indeed, every \(a+b\) divides \(P(A)\), and (15) follows by averaging (11) over the \(|A|\) rows.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Gcd normalization and control by a small anchor set
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

For a finite set \(B\) containing positive integers, put
\[
 g_B=\gcd\{b:b\in B\},\qquad
 B^{\rm prim}=\{b/g_B:b\in B\},
\]
and define its normalized height by
\[
 H_B=\max_{b\in B} b/g_B.
\]
Division by \(g_B\) is injective on \(B\), so \(|B^{\rm prim}|=|B|\). If \(|B|\ge2\), then \(g_B>0\), the normalized set has gcd \(1\), and \(H_B>0\).

We first relate \(H_B\) to gcd-distance. Fix \(a\in B\). Then
\[
 \log H_B\le2\sum_{b\in B}d(a,b).                                   \tag{16}
\]
To justify this, first observe the divisibility
\[
 \frac a{\gcd(a,g_B)}\mid
 \prod_{b\in B}\frac a{\gcd(a,b)}.

a\]
It follows prime by prime, or inductively using the relation between gcd and lcm. Since \(g_B\mid a\), the left side is \(a/g_B\). Taking logarithms and using \(\gcd(a,b)\le b\), we obtain
\[
 \log(a/g_B)
 \le\sum_{b\in B}(\log a-\log\gcd(a,b))
 \le\sum_{b\in B}d(a,b).                                           \tag{17}
\]
For any \(b\in B\),
\[
 \log(b/g_B)
 =\log b-\log g_B
 \le (\log a-\log g_B)+d(a,b).
\]
The first term is bounded by (17), and the individual nonnegative term \(d(a,b)\) is at most the full sum. Thus
\[
 \log(b/g_B)\le2\sum_{c\in B}d(a,c).
\]
Taking the maximum over \(b\) proves (16).

We also need a simple low-weight selection fact. If nonnegative weights \(w(x)\) are placed on a finite set \(A\), and \(2m\le|A|\), then there is a subset \(B\subseteq A\) of size \(m\) such that
\[
 |A|\sum_{b\in B}w(b)\le2m\sum_{a\in A}w(a).                        \tag{18}
\]
Indeed, at least \(m\) points satisfy
\(|A|w(x)\le2\sum_Aw\); otherwise more than \(|A|/2\) points violate this inequality, and their weights alone would sum to more than the total. Choose any \(m\) of the good points and sum their inequalities.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
5. The exceptional-prime pigeonhole argument
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

For a finite set of primes \(S\) and \(D>0\), define the prime box
\[
 \Pi(S,D)=\prod_{p\in S}p^{\lfloor\log_pD\rfloor}.
\]
Then
\[
 \Pi(S,D)\le D^{|S|},                                                \tag{19}
\]
and every positive \(S\)-smooth integer at most \(D\) divides \(\Pi(S,D)\).

We use the following pigeonhole lemma. Let \(F_b\), indexed by a finite set \(B\), be nonzero \(S\)-smooth integers. Suppose
\[
 \gcd(F_b,F_c)\mid M\quad(b\ne c),
\]
where \(M>0\). If \(|B|>|S|\), then some \(F_b\) divides \(M\).

For if no \(F_b\) divides \(M\), then for every \(b\) there is a prime \(p_b\in S\) with
\[
 v_{p_b}(F_b)>v_{p_b}(M).
\]
Two different indices cannot choose the same prime: if \(p_b=p_c=p\), then \(p^{v_p(M)+1}\) divides both \(F_b,F_c\), hence their gcd and therefore \(M\), a contradiction. Thus \(b\mapsto p_b\) is an injection from \(B\) into \(S\), contrary to \(|B|>|S|\).

Now suppose \(B\) is a set of positive integers at most \(H\), \(S\) is a set of primes, \(u>0\), and \(\gcd(t,u)=1\). Assume each
\[
 F_b=t+ub
\]
is \(S\)-smooth and \(|B|>|S|\). Then
\[
 t+u\le H^{|S|}.                                                     \tag{20}
\]
For distinct \(b,c\),
\[
 \gcd(t+ub,t+uc)\mid |b-c|.                                         \tag{21}
\]
Indeed, the gcd divides \(u|b-c|\), and it is coprime to \(u\), because \(\gcd(t,u)=1\). Since \(|b-c|\le H\) and all its relevant prime factors lie in \(S\), (21) implies that this gcd divides \(\Pi(S,H)\). The pigeonhole lemma supplies a \(b\) for which
\(t+ub\mid\Pi(S,H)\). Since \(b\ge1\),
\[
 t+u\le t+ub\le\Pi(S,H)\le H^{|S|},
\]
proving (20).

We apply this to a scaled anchor set. Let \(A\) be a finite set of positive integers, let \(B\) consist of positive integers at most \(H\), and suppose
\[
 \{gb:b\in B\}\subseteq A,
\]
where \(g>0\). Put \(S\) equal to the prime support of \(P(A)\), and \(r=|S|\). If
\[
 |B|\ge r+2,                                                         \tag{22}
\]
then for every \(x\in A\),
\[
 \frac{x}{\gcd(x,g)}+\frac g{\gcd(x,g)}\le H^r.                     \tag{23}
\]
To prove this, set \(h=\gcd(x,g)\), \(t=x/h\), and \(u=g/h\). Then \(\gcd(t,u)=1\). Remove from \(B\), if present, the single value \(x/g\); the remaining set still has more than \(r\) elements. For each remaining \(b\), the elements \(x\) and \(gb\) of \(A\) are distinct, so every prime factor of \(x+gb\) lies in \(S\). Since
\[
 x+gb=h(t+ub),
\]
all prime factors of \(t+ub\) also lie in \(S\). Formula (20) now gives (23).

Assume additionally that \(A\) is primitive, meaning \(\gcd(A)=1\). Then the scaled anchors force a global height bound:
\[
 x\le H^{r(r+1)}\qquad(x\in A).                                     \tag{24}
\]
First, the prime factors of \(g\) all lie in \(S\): choose two distinct \(b,c\in B\), possible by (22); then \(g\mid gb+gc\), and the latter is an off-diagonal sum from \(A\).

From (23), in particular,
\[
 g/\gcd(x,g)\le H^r\qquad(x\in A).                                  \tag{25}
\]
For each prime \(p\mid g\), primitivity of \(A\) supplies an \(x\in A\) not divisible by \(p\). Hence the full prime-power \(p^{v_p(g)}\) survives in \(g/\gcd(x,g)\), and (25) yields
\[
 p^{v_p(g)}\le H^r.
\]
Multiplying this over the at most \(r\) prime divisors of \(g\) gives
\[
 g\le(H^r)^r.
\]
Also (23) gives \(x/\gcd(x,g)\le H^r\). Therefore
\[
 x=\gcd(x,g)\frac{x}{\gcd(x,g)}
 \le gH^r\le H^{r^2+r},
\]
which is (24).

More generally, suppose \(C\subseteq A\), \(A\) is primitive, every element of \(C\) is positive, and \(|C|\ge r+2\). Taking \(g=g_C\), \(B=C^{\rm prim}\), and \(H=H_C\), the scaled set \(gB\) is exactly \(C\). Thus (24) gives
\[
 x\le H_C^{r(r+1)}\qquad(x\in A).                                  \tag{26}
\]

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Eliminating height: the polynomial estimate for primitive sets
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

Let \(A\) now be a finite primitive set of positive integers. Put
\[
 r=r(A),\qquad m=r+2,
\]
and let \(H=\max A\). We prove
\[
 |A|\le64(r+1)^5.                                                    \tag{27}
\]

If \(|A|<2m=2(r+2)\), then (27) is immediate (indeed the right side is much larger for every \(r\ge0\)). We may therefore assume
\[
 2m\le|A|.                                                           \tag{28}
\]
This implies \(|A|\ge4\), and because \(A\) consists of distinct positive integers, \(H\ge2\). In particular \(\log H>0\), and
\[
 \log(2H)=\log2+\log H\le2\log H.                                  \tag{29}
\]

Choose \(a\in A\) satisfying the row bound (15):
\[
 \sum_{b\in A}d(a,b)\le4r^2\log(2H).                                \tag{30}
\]
Apply (18) with weights \(w(b)=d(a,b)\) and size \(m\). We obtain \(B\subseteq A\), \(|B|=m\), with
\[
 |A|\sum_{b\in B}d(a,b)
 \le2m\sum_{b\in A}d(a,b).                                         \tag{31}
\]
Let
\[
 C=B\cup\{a\}.
\]
Then \(C\subseteq A\), \(|C|\ge m=r+2\), and, since \(d(a,a)=0\),
\[
 \sum_{c\in C}d(a,c)=\sum_{b\in B}d(a,b).                          \tag{32}
\]
By (16),
\[
 \log H_C\le2\sum_{b\in B}d(a,b).
\]
Multiplying by \(|A|\), then using (31) and (30), gives
\[
 |A|\log H_C
 \le4m\sum_{b\in A}d(a,b)
 \le16mr^2\log(2H).                                                 \tag{33}
\]

Because \(C\subseteq A\), \(|C|\ge r+2\), and \(A\) is primitive, (26) applies. In particular, taking the largest member of \(A\),
\[
 H\le H_C^{r(r+1)}.
\]
Taking logarithms,
\[
 \log H\le r(r+1)\log H_C.                                         \tag{34}
\]
Multiply (34) by \(|A|\) and use (33):
\[
 |A|\log H
 \le16m r^3(r+1)\log(2H).
\]
By (29) and \(\log H>0\), cancellation yields
\[
 |A|\le32m r^3(r+1)=32(r+2)r^3(r+1).
\]
Finally, \(r+2\le2(r+1)\) and \(r^3\le(r+1)^3\), so
\[
 |A|\le64(r+1)^5.
\]
This proves (27), including the case \(r=0\) (under the large-set assumption the displayed inequalities would force an impossibility, while the small-set case was already handled).

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Removing zero and the common gcd
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

We now prove (1) for an arbitrary finite \(A\subseteq\mathbb N\). Remove zero and write
\[
 B=A\setminus\{0\}.
\]
Then \(|A|\le|B|+1\), and all elements of \(B\) are positive. If \(|B|<2\), (1) is immediate.

Otherwise let \(g=\gcd(B)>0\) and
\[
 C=B^{\rm prim}=\{b/g:b\in B\}.
\]
Then \(|C|=|B|\), all elements of \(C\) are positive, and \(\gcd(C)=1\). Moreover,
\[
 P(B)=g^{|B|(|B|-1)}P(C),
\]
because every ordered off-diagonal sum in \(B\) is \(g\) times the corresponding sum in \(C\). Thus \(P(C)\mid P(B)\), so every prime factor of \(P(C)\) is a prime factor of \(P(B)\). Also \(B\subseteq A\), hence \(P(B)\mid P(A)\), because the former product is a subproduct of the latter. Therefore
\[
 r(C)\le r(A).
\]
Applying (27) to \(C\),
\[
 |B|=|C|\le64(r(C)+1)^5\le64(r(A)+1)^5.
\]
Since \((r(A)+1)^5\ge1\),
\[
 |A|\le |B|+1
 \le64(r(A)+1)^5+1
 \le65(r(A)+1)^5.
\]
This is (1).

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
8. Uniform superlogarithmic growth
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

We claim that for every real \(K\) there is an integer \(N\) such that every finite \(A\subseteq\mathbb N\) with \(|A|\ge N\) satisfies
\[
 K\log|A|<r(A).                                                      \tag{35}
\]

Let
\[
 D=65(K+1)^5.
\]
The standard estimate \((\log n)^5/n\to0\) implies
\[
 D\frac{(\log n)^5}{n}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Also \(\log n\ge1\) eventually. Hence, for all sufficiently large \(n\),
\[
 D(\log n)^5<n.                                                      \tag{36}
\]
Suppose, contrary to (35), that for such an \(A\), with \(n=|A|\), we had
\[
 r(A)\le K\log n.
\]
Since \(\log n\ge1\),
\[
 r(A)+1\le(K+1)\log n.
\]
(The existence of the nonnegative left side also makes the right side nonnegative in any case in which this supposition is possible.) Raising to the fifth power and applying (1),
\[
 n\le65(r(A)+1)^5
 \le65(K+1)^5(\log n)^5
 =D(\log n)^5,
\]
contradicting (36). Thus (35) holds.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
9. Passage to the maximal function
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

Let \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) satisfy the stated maximality condition. Thus, for each \(n\), \(f(n)\) is the greatest integer \(m\) such that
\[
 m\le r(A)
\]
for every finite \(A\subseteq\mathbb N\) of cardinality \(n\).

To prove that \(f(n)/\log n\to+\infty\), fix an arbitrary real \(K\). Choose \(N\) as in (35), and take
\[
 n\ge\max(N,2).
\]
Then \(\log n>0\). For every set \(A\) of cardinality \(n\), (35) says
\[
 K\log n<r(A).
\]
Let \(m\) be the least nonnegative integer at least \(K\log n\). Since \(r(A)\) is an integer and is strictly greater than \(K\log n\), we have
\[
 m\le r(A)
\]
for every such \(A\). Thus \(m\) has the universal property appearing in the definition of \(f(n)\). By maximality,
\[
 m\le f(n).
\]
Since \(K\log n\le m\), it follows that
\[
 K\log n\le f(n).
\]
Dividing by the positive number \(\log n\) gives
\[
 K\le\frac{f(n)}{\log n}.
\]
For every real \(K\), this inequality holds for all sufficiently large \(n\). This is precisely
\[
 \frac{f(n)}{\log n}\longrightarrow+\infty.
\]
Hence the conjectured statement holds.
